blocks.content: Instead of waiting for the complete response, you receive tokens one by one as they're generated. Allows for a more responsive UX.

blocks.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

with client.messages.stream(
    model="claude-opus-4-8",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Tell me a joke"}]
) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)

blocks.content: Messages API streaming is Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTP, not WebSockets. The difference isn't a technicality: they're two different transport primitives for two different problems.

rows.value: Plain HTTP, a single long-lived response
A request that triggers one long response — exactly the shape of a message to Claude
Bidirectional: either side can send at any time
A separate persistent connection with its own handshake
Real-time messaging where the client also pushes data without having made a new request — multi-user chat, live collaboration

blocks.title: Where a WebSocket does fit into a Claude-powered app
blocks.content: Not for talking to the Anthropic API — that's always HTTP + SSE. A WebSocket shows up in the layer between your backend and the end user's browser, when the application needs to push events to the client that aren't the response to that client's own request (notifications from other users, shared state in a collaborative session). The typical pattern: your server consumes Claude's SSE stream and re-emits those same chunks over the WebSocket it already keeps open with the browser.

Beyond the token counts returned with every response (`usage.input_tokens`, `usage.output_tokens`), Anthropic exposes a dedicated Admin API to monitor consumption and cost across an entire organization: the same data shown on the Usage and Cost pages of Claude Console, but programmable. It requires Admin API credentials — a regular workspace API key isn't enough.

rows: Token consumption by time bucket (1m/1h/1d), filterable and groupable by model, workspace, API key, service tier, or `speed` (fast mode)
Cost in USD, groupable by workspace or description — daily granularity only

blocks.title: Code execution doesn't show up in the usage endpoint
blocks.content: Code execution cost is only visible in the Cost Report, grouped under the "Code Execution Usage" description — the Usage Report doesn't include it. Conversely, Priority Tier shows up in usage (by filtering `service_tier=priority`) but not in the Cost Report, which uses a different billing model.

articles.title: stop_reason, advanced streaming, and dead-letter queues

blocks.content: Every API response includes a stop_reason field indicating why generation ended. In production systems, stop_reason is the first diagnostic signal when behavior is unexpected. Ignoring it is a design mistake.

rows: The model finished its response naturally.
The response was truncated because it hit the max_tokens limit.
Increase max_tokens or redesign for shorter outputs. NEVER treat the output as complete.
The model is invoking a tool. Wait for the result before continuing.
Execute the tool, return the result, continue the multi-turn loop.
Generation ended after hitting a configured stop sequence.
The model paused its turn (Extended Thinking enabled).
Continue the loop with the same message history.

blocks.title: Unchecked max_tokens produces silently incomplete outputs
blocks.content: If stop_reason is "max_tokens", the output is truncated. A pipeline that doesn't check this field can process incomplete JSON, partial analyses, or cut-off lists as if they were valid results. Checking stop_reason should be part of the contract for any call that produces structured output.

blocks.code:
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=4096,
    messages=messages
)

if response.stop_reason == "max_tokens":
    # Truncated output — don't continue as if it were valid
    raise OutputTruncatedError(
        f"Response truncated at {response.usage.output_tokens} tokens. "
        "Increase max_tokens or split the task."
    )
elif response.stop_reason == "tool_use":
    # Process tool calls and continue the loop
    tool_result = execute_tools(response.content)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": tool_result})

blocks.content: In streaming, the model can emit a tool_use block in the middle of the response. The client must detect this event and pause processing until it executes the tool and returns its result. If the client simply keeps consuming the stream while ignoring the tool_use, the model doesn't have the tool result and the response ends up incomplete or incoherent.

items.title: The model starts streaming
items.description: The client receives text chunks normally.

items.title: tool_use event detected
items.description: The stream emits a block of type tool_use with the tool name and its arguments. This is the cutoff point.

items.title: Pause stream consumption
items.description: The client stops consuming the stream and executes the tool locally.

items.title: Return the result as tool_result
items.description: The client returns the tool's result in a new message of type tool_result.

items.title: The model continues
items.description: With the result available, the model continues generating its response. Streaming can resume.

blocks.title: 2% mid-stream interruptions are normal under high latency
blocks.content: In production, ~2% of streams can be interrupted by network timeouts, instance restarts, or transient instability. The fix isn't to eliminate streaming but to implement retry with reconnection: on detecting an interruption, retry from the last known checkpoint (not from the start of the message). If the stream is interrupted after a tool_use but before the result, the retry must include the tool_result in the history.

A dead-letter queue (DLQ) is a separate queue where requests that exhausted their retry budget without success get sent. In high-volume agentic pipelines (payments, document processing, data extraction), the DLQ is the mechanism that guarantees no request is silently lost: failed items remain available for human review or manual reprocessing.

rows.value: Discarded. The system has no record of the failure.
The transaction disappears — neither approved nor rejected. The customer gets no confirmation.
The team discovers the problem days later from data inconsistencies.
Moved to the DLQ with full context: original payload, number of attempts, last error.
The transaction stays in review. The team can process it manually or requeue it.
Immediate alert. The DLQ is observable and has volume metrics.

blocks.title: The DLQ must include the original idempotency_key
blocks.content: When DLQ items are reprocessed manually or in a second pipeline, they must use the same idempotency_key from the original request. This guarantees that if the original request partially executed before failing, reprocessing doesn't produce duplicates. Without the idempotency_key, the DLQ creates a new vector for duplicates.

items.title: Full payload
items.description: The DLQ must store the complete original request, not just the ID. The operations team needs the payload to diagnose and eventually reprocess.

items.title: Idempotency key
items.description: Always include the original idempotency_key so reprocessing is safe against duplicates.

items.title: Metrics and alerts
items.description: A DLQ with no alert doesn't exist operationally. Configure an alarm when volume exceeds the expected threshold (e.g., >0.1% of requests).

items.title: Requeue carefully
items.description: Before requeuing DLQ items, verify the error was transient and not structural (invalid schema, user doesn't exist). Requeuing a 422 error creates an infinite loop back to the DLQ.
